whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes that the wax lays down one pair of layers per year and locks in the hormones circulating at that moment, and the second sentence says the plug can be read "decade by decade." The blank therefore needs a word for a record that preserves events in their time order. A chronicle is exactly that: an account that runs through time in sequence.

whyWrong.B: A summary compresses information and drops the sequence, which is the opposite of what the passage values in the plug — the year-by-year ordering is the whole point.
whyWrong.C: A forecast points forward to what has not happened yet; the wax records stress the animal has already experienced.
whyWrong.D: A symptom is a single present-time sign of a condition, not a record covering an entire lifespan.

tips: When a sentence ends with a phrase like "decade by decade" or "year after year," the blank almost always needs a word meaning an ordered record.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts the blank with "fixed by any external standard," and the preceding sentences say each set is tuned only to itself so that an outside instrument clashes with it. The blank needs a word meaning belonging to that one ensemble alone. "Peculiar to" carries precisely that sense of exclusive belonging.

whyWrong.A: Indifferent would say tuning does not care about the ensemble, reversing the relationship the passage describes.
whyWrong.B: Adjacent means physically next to something; it says nothing about ownership or exclusivity.
whyWrong.C: Secondary would rank tuning as less important than something else, but the passage is about where the standard comes from, not about priority.

commonMistakes: Reading "peculiar" only as "strange" and rejecting it; in this construction it means "belonging exclusively to."

whyCorrect: The blank sits after "not fixed but," so it must mean the opposite of fixed, and the clause that follows spells out the sense wanted: "shifting a little with each generation." Mutable means liable to change. It matches both the contrast and the trailing description.

whyWrong.A: Static is a synonym for fixed, so it contradicts the "not fixed but" structure.
whyWrong.C: Obsolete means no longer in use, but the passage says the tradition has been kept alive for centuries.
whyWrong.D: Uniform would mean the same everywhere, which the passage denies when it says two nearby villages harmonise the song differently.

whyCorrect: Before the case, losing nearly every specimen was the norm; the colon then gives evidence that survival became dependable — ferns living eight months at sea, and the return trip going the same way. The blank needs a word for something that now happens as a matter of course. Routine says survival became the ordinary outcome rather than the exception.

whyWrong.A: Incidental means minor or beside the point, but survival is the very thing the case was judged on.
whyWrong.B: Negotiable means open to bargaining, which makes no sense applied to whether plants live.
whyWrong.D: Miraculous would mark survival as inexplicable and rare, but the evidence after the colon is of survival happening reliably and repeatedly.

whyCorrect: Read the sentence for what is physically being done: the capital is cut by a carver, it has acanthus leaves that chip in transport, and the carver studies the standing shaft before undercutting it. Only a piece of carved stone at the top of a column fits all three facts. The context is architectural, not financial or typographic.

whyWrong.A: A seat of government cannot be cut by a carver or chipped in transport.
whyWrong.B: Wealth used to generate wealth is the economics sense; nothing here concerns money, and wealth has no acanthus leaves.
whyWrong.D: An uppercase letter is the typographic sense, which has no bearing on quarrying and column shafts.

tips: For these items, ignore the word's most familiar meaning and test each sense against the concrete verbs attached to it in the sentence.

whyCorrect: The sentences before the underlined one describe what the sphere is and how it works. The underlined sentence does two things after that: it gives a number for how much sway is removed, and it says what that number means in practice, the gap between a nuisance and an evacuation. So its function is to measure the effect and explain the stakes.

whyWrong.A: No second problem is introduced; the sentence closes off the one problem the text opened with.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in it casts doubt on the sphere — the forty per cent figure confirms the device works.
whyWrong.C: The method of suspension was already given earlier, in the phrase about cables; the underlined sentence never returns to it.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence gives a hard condition on the process: strip the bark in early summer while the sap runs, or the fibre cannot be obtained at all. The rest of the paragraph then follows the material through soaking, splitting, spinning and dyeing. Within that sequence, this sentence's job is to set the limit on when the process can even begin.

whyWrong.A: No other fibre is mentioned anywhere in the text, so no comparison or claim of superiority is being made.
whyWrong.B: The resemblance to woodcarving appears in the final sentence and is never explained; this sentence is about harvest timing.
whyWrong.C: Only one method of preparing bark is described, so there is nothing being contrasted.

whyCorrect: The final sentence gives two reasons and pairs each with a payoff: different species lived in different intervals, which yields a calendar, and skeleton shape reflects the water the animal grew in, which yields a thermometer. The answer has to carry both halves. Species turnover marking time and shape indicating past conditions is that pair restated.

whyWrong.A: The text never compares silica with carbonate or says anything about ease of dating.
whyWrong.B: "Only fossils that survive" is far stronger than the text, which merely says these skeletons accumulate on the deep seafloor.
whyWrong.D: The passage says the ooze piles up over millions of years, which rules out year-to-year resolution rather than supporting it.

whyCorrect: Every sentence builds toward the last one: the characters differ from the school script, they encode local speech by sound, and women shut out of the official script could still read each other. The main idea has to combine the independence from the official script with the fact that it let women communicate. That is what the first option states.

whyWrong.B: The scarcity of paper is never mentioned; the text reports the fans and handkerchiefs without giving a cause.
whyWrong.C: The text says the characters were not what boys were taught, which is not the same as men being forbidden to learn them.
whyWrong.D: The text explicitly says these are not the school characters, so calling it a decorative variant of them contradicts the passage.

whyCorrect: Solheim's claim has two parts to be supported: the ivory market collapsed, and that collapse, not the climate, drove the abandonment. Evidence that hay yields were still normal right up to the end removes the rival explanation, and evidence that the price collapse came before the departures puts the cause in the right order relative to the effect. Doing both is what makes this the strongest support.

whyWrong.A: Iceland is a different colony with a different economy; its farms surviving says nothing about why Greenland's ivory trade mattered.
whyWrong.B: Colder summers are the rival climate explanation, so this supports the other side of the dispute.
whyWrong.D: The distance to the hunting grounds concerns how the ivory was obtained, not whether losing its market ended the settlements.

tips: For support questions with a named rival explanation, the best evidence usually knocks the rival down and confirms the timing at the same time.

whyCorrect: The two explanations differ in what pitch depends on: Novak says it tracks noise, the alternative says it tracks body size. Body size does not change from minute to minute, so a bird that raises its pitch within minutes of traffic getting louder can only be responding to the noise. That observation fits Novak and is impossible under the size explanation.

whyWrong.A: Lighter city birds is exactly what the alternative explanation predicts, so it favours the rival rather than Novak.
whyWrong.C: That traffic noise is low-frequency is already assumed in Novak's setup; it establishes the premise but does not decide between the two accounts, since size-driven pitch would look the same.
whyWrong.D: Territory size is a separate behaviour with no stated link to either song pitch or noise.

whyCorrect: The conservator's whole case rests on treating invisible joins as evidence that there were no joins. To undermine it you need a reason the joins could be absent from view while still existing. Showing that comparable figures had their joins filed down and disguised, detectable only by X-ray, does exactly that: the surface evidence no longer distinguishes a single pour from a disguised assembly.

whyWrong.A: A uniform alloy is at worst neutral and if anything consistent with one pour, so it does not weaken the argument.
whyWrong.B: Technical feasibility makes the single pour more plausible, not less.
whyWrong.C: A separately cast base concerns a different component and leaves the claim about the body untouched.

commonMistakes: Looking for a fact that contradicts the conclusion directly, when the task is to break the link between the stated evidence and the conclusion.

whyCorrect: The researchers only sampled moths that had already gathered at the lights, so the sample was selected by the very behaviour under study. The conditional sentence then supposes that tight spiralling and attraction to light go together in the same moths. If that is so, the tighter spirals could be a property of which moths turned up, with the light doing nothing to their flight at all.

whyWrong.A: Nothing supports a reversal; switching the lights off is a different experiment, not a consequence of the sampling problem.
whyWrong.B: The unlit fields were the comparison group and were not the site of the sampling problem; the bias is on the lit side.
whyWrong.C: This asserts the causal conclusion the sampling problem is precisely calling into question.

tips: When a text points out how a sample was collected, the completion is nearly always about a limit on what the data can show, not a stronger conclusion.

whyCorrect: The Linear B case sets the standard: sound values counted as a decipherment only because they produced meaningful words in a known language. Linear A takes the same sign values and produces nothing identifiable in any language. So the signs can be given sounds, but the sounds do not resolve into a language anyone recognises.

whyWrong.B: The text says applying the Greek values to Linear A yields no identifiable words, which is the direct denial of this.
whyWrong.C: Damage is never mentioned; the problem is that readable signs give unreadable words.
whyWrong.D: Chariot and sheep inventories are the Linear B content; the passage never says what Linear A texts contain, and cannot, since they are not understood.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "Because," which makes everything through "room temperature" a subordinate clause; the main clause is "two starters ... will drift apart." A subordinate clause that comes first is separated from the main clause by a comma, and nothing stronger. So the comma is the only correct mark here.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and "Because the balance ... responds to flour, water and room temperature" cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.B: A colon also requires an independent clause in front of it, and the "Because" clause is not one; the second half is not an explanation or list being introduced, either.
whyWrong.C: Adding "and" makes "two starters ... will drift apart" read as a second thing the balance responds to, which garbles the sentence and leaves it without a main clause.

tips: Cover the part before the blank: if it cannot stand as its own sentence, a semicolon or colon is automatically out.

whyCorrect: What follows the blank is "each of which can be matched to a dated eruption" — a relative clause built on "which," so it cannot stand as a sentence. A non-essential relative clause attaches to the main clause with a comma. That leaves the comma as the only workable mark.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and the "each of which" clause is a fragment.
whyWrong.B: A colon likewise needs to introduce something after a complete statement, and a relative clause is not what a colon introduces.
whyWrong.C: A period creates an outright fragment, and it also leaves the following word incorrectly lowercased.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences: "Ingots ... have been traced ... to mines in Central Asia" and "the metal had travelled some three thousand kilometres." Two independent clauses need a semicolon, a period, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction. Only the semicolon is offered.

whyWrong.A: Running the two clauses together with no punctuation is a fused sentence.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by "and" is not a construction English uses; the colon already does the joining, so the conjunction is redundant and ungrammatical.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: "It fills its pond as the tide floods and works the stones as the tide ebbs" is one complete sentence, and "the wheel turns for roughly five hours out of every twelve" is another. When "and" joins two independent clauses, the conjunction takes a comma in front of it. That gives comma plus "and."

whyWrong.A: A colon cannot sit in front of a coordinating conjunction, and nothing here is being introduced or itemised.
whyWrong.B: With no comma, "and the wheel turns" reads at first as a third thing the mill does, and joining two full clauses with a bare "and" is not the convention being tested.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon plus "and" doubles up two ways of joining clauses; use one or the other, not both.

whyCorrect: Strip the prepositional phrase out of the subject: the subject is "Each," not "segments." "Each" is singular no matter what follows it, so the verb must be singular. "Has" is the singular present form.

whyWrong.A: "Have" is plural and agrees with "segments," the object of "of," which can never be the subject of the sentence.
whyWrong.C: "Having" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence would be left with no main verb at all.
whyWrong.D: "Were having" is both plural and in the past progressive, which clashes with the present-tense description in the sentence before it.

commonMistakes: Letting the nearest noun decide the verb; "each of the ... segments" is singular.

whyCorrect: The comparison is between two amounts of rainfall, so the blank must stand in for the singular noun "rainfall" and be followed by the modifier "recorded at the station on the leeward side." The pronoun that does that job is "that." Written out, it means nearly three times the rainfall recorded on the leeward side.

whyWrong.B: "Those" is plural, but the thing being compared is a single quantity, "the annual rainfall."
whyWrong.C: "It" cannot take a following participial modifier in this construction, and it points back to the windward figure rather than standing in for a second one.
whyWrong.D: "Which" would open a relative clause describing the windward rainfall, which destroys the comparison the sentence is making.

whyCorrect: The sentence is inverted: the prepositional phrase "Beneath the cathedral floor" comes first and the subject, "the foundations," follows the verb. The subject is plural, so the verb must be plural. "Lie" is the plural present form.

whyWrong.A: "Has lain" is singular and so disagrees with the plural "foundations."
whyWrong.B: "Lies" is the singular form, agreeing with nothing in the sentence — "floor" is inside a prepositional phrase and cannot be the subject.
whyWrong.D: "Lying" is a participle, leaving the sentence without a finite verb.

tips: When a sentence starts with a place phrase, find the subject after the verb before choosing the number.

whyCorrect: The first sentence reports what a bog preserves: skin, hair, stomach contents. The second reports what it destroys — the same acids dissolve the bones. That is a reversal of the expectation the first sentence sets up, so the transition has to signal contrast.

whyWrong.A: "Thus" claims the bone loss follows logically from the preservation of skin and hair, but the sentence is presenting it as the opposite of that.
whyWrong.B: "For instance" would make bone loss an example of preservation, which it is not.
whyWrong.C: "In fact" intensifies or confirms the previous statement; here the second sentence limits it instead.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general claim about sensitivity, that the device detects fields a billion times fainter than Earth's. The second names one specific thing that sensitivity allows: reading the field of a single nerve. A specific case offered in support of a general claim takes an exemplifying transition.

whyWrong.B: "In contrast" requires the two sentences to differ, but the second confirms the first.
whyWrong.C: "Instead" replaces a rejected alternative, and no alternative has been raised.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" signals that the second statement holds despite the first, when in fact it follows straight from it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a requirement — insulation that survives years of cold, pressure and salt water. The second gives the engineers' response to that requirement, wrapping the core in a latex that stays flexible in exactly those conditions. The link is problem to solution, so the transition must express cause.

whyWrong.A: "In summary" announces a recap, but the gutta-percha detail is new information, not a restatement.
whyWrong.C: "Even so" signals concession, implying the wrapping happened despite the requirement rather than because of it.
whyWrong.D: "By comparison" sets two things side by side, and only one material is under discussion.

whyCorrect: The goal names two things: what the sewers changed, and what followed from that change. Only one option supplies both — the rerouting of waste to downstream outfalls instead of the central Thames, and the sharp fall in cholera deaths afterwards. The others each give a single note.

whyWrong.A: The curtains at Parliament describe the conditions before the sewers, not what the sewers changed.
whyWrong.C: Bazalgette's authorisation is background about who was appointed, and it names no change to the river and no result.
whyWrong.D: The foulness of the Thames is the starting problem, so it addresses neither half of the stated goal.

tips: When a synthesis goal names two things, cross out every option that delivers only one.

whyCorrect: The goal is a design point: the record had to be usable by a finder with no language in common with its makers. The note that answers that is the one about playing instructions etched as diagrams, since diagrams work without shared language. The chosen option states the design problem and the feature that answers it in a single sentence.

whyWrong.A: The disc's material and launch date say nothing about how a finder would understand it.
whyWrong.C: Greetings in 55 languages is content that assumes language, which works against the point being emphasised rather than for it.
whyWrong.D: Where the probes are now is unrelated to how the record was designed to be understood.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for the mechanism: how a net turns fog into water. The only note describing a mechanism is condensation on the threads and drainage into a gutter, and the chosen option pairs that process with the yield it produces. That is an explanation of how, not merely of where or how much.

whyWrong.A: The yield alone reports an outcome and skips the process the goal asks about.
whyWrong.B: A description of the panels and their location tells you what a fog net is, not how it makes water.
whyWrong.D: The brewery is a use for the water once collected, which is downstream of the question asked.

whyCorrect: The method described is passive measurement: detectors count muons and an excess from one direction means less rock that way. The closing phrase "without a single block being moved" rules out anything that touches the structure. The blank therefore needs a word for finding something out, and detect is that word.

whyWrong.A: Reinforce means to strengthen physically, which contradicts the point that nothing in the pyramid is disturbed.
whyWrong.B: Dating gives an age; muon counts give the thickness of rock along a path, not a date.
whyWrong.C: Excavating means digging the void out, the very thing the last clause says does not happen.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence supplies the mechanism: salt pulls water out of organic material and stops decay. The blank then contrasts with "would long ago have rotted away," so it must name the opposite outcome. Preserved is the word for material kept from decaying.

whyWrong.B: Discarded describes how the objects got there, not what the salt did to them, and it does not contrast with rotting.
whyWrong.C: Compressed refers to being squeezed, which is not what removing water and halting decay does.
whyWrong.D: Buried is true but says nothing about survival — objects that rot are buried too, so it loses the contrast the sentence sets up.

commonMistakes: Choosing a word that is factually true of the situation rather than the one the sentence's contrast requires.

whyCorrect: The sentence after the colon explains the term for you: below a certain depth the hull grounds on the silt. That makes draft a property of the vessel measured against water depth. The reading that fits is the depth of water a vessel needs in order to float.

whyWrong.A: A current of air has nothing to do with hulls grounding on silt.
whyWrong.C: A demand for payment is the banking sense and does not explain why a bigger vessel cannot pass.
whyWrong.D: A preliminary document version cannot be described as greater or lesser in a way that grounds a hull.

whyCorrect: The animal stops metabolising altogether and can be restarted decades later by water, so life is neither ended nor continuing — it is halted and resumable. The sentence sets that against "not sleep," asking for something more complete than sleep but still reversible. A suspension is exactly a temporary halt that can be lifted.

whyWrong.B: A repudiation is a rejection, a word for an attitude rather than a physiological state.
whyWrong.C: Celebration makes no sense applied to a dormant animal and clashes with the whole description.
whyWrong.D: Prolongation would mean life continuing longer, but the passage says metabolism stops entirely.

whyCorrect: The blank is filled out by the clause after the comma: the soil was built up from charcoal, fish bone and pottery that people threw away. The contrast with the earlier assumption of a natural formation means the word must attribute the soil to human activity. Anthropogenic means produced by humans.

whyWrong.A: Transient means short-lived, but this soil accumulated over centuries and is still there.
whyWrong.C: Sedimentary describes deposition by natural processes, which is the assumption the sentence is overturning.
whyWrong.D: Volcanic names a natural origin as well, and nothing in the list of ingredients comes from an eruption.

whyCorrect: Track the text sentence by sentence: the first says what a kgotla is, the second and third describe how speaking and hearing proceed, and the last narrows down what the chief may and may not do. That is a definition, then a procedure, then a limit on the leader. No other option matches that three-part movement.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text is dated or sequenced historically; it describes a standing practice, not a development.
whyWrong.B: No criticism is ever raised, so there is nothing for the text to rebut.
whyWrong.D: Only one kind of assembly is described, so no comparison is made and no fairness claim is argued.

whyCorrect: Every detail serves one line of argument: the earliest tablets are records of barley, beer and livestock, and the signs come from debt tokens pressed into clay envelopes. The last sentence closes the chain by showing how the impressions replaced the tokens. The purpose is to explain how writing grew out of record-keeping.

whyWrong.B: The opening only notes that writing did not start with poetry; it makes no claim about how literature has been valued.
whyWrong.C: Firing and storage are never mentioned; the clay details concern envelopes and impressions.
whyWrong.D: No alphabet appears in the text, so there is no comparison to draw.

whyCorrect: The last sentence states the point outright: what sank the ship is also what saved her. The details before it explain how — brackish harbour water kept out the shipworm, and the mud kept out oxygen, both conditions of the very place she went down in. The main idea has to join the sinking and the preservation.

whyWrong.A: "All waters" overstates the text, which limits the shipworm claim to open salt water and specifically excludes the Baltic.
whyWrong.B: Only one vessel is discussed; the text never says the harbour holds others.
whyWrong.C: The text says the carvings came up still crisp, which is preservation, not later recarving.

whyCorrect: The final sentence answers the question directly and then rules out the tempting alternative: perfumers valued the material because it held other scents on the skin for hours longer, "not for any quality of its own smell." So the reason is a fixative effect on other scents.

whyWrong.A: The change in smell happens over years of drifting, not over a day, and the text says its own smell was not the reason.
whyWrong.B: The text never ranks its strength, and aged ambergris is described as only faintly sweet.
whyWrong.D: Fresh material is described as foul-smelling, and nothing is said about the quantities gathered.

whyCorrect: Duarte's claim has two sides: profile decides the tone, and tin content does not. A test that holds the profile constant while letting tin content vary isolates exactly that. If those bells sound nearly identical, the alloy variation is shown not to matter, which is the harder half of her claim.

whyWrong.B: Hardness and brittleness are mechanical properties; the claim is about pitch and tone, and nothing links the two here.
whyWrong.C: Secrecy about recipes explains founders' behaviour but tests neither factor's effect on sound.
whyWrong.D: Cooling time is a fact about casting large bells and bears on neither profile nor alloy as a cause of tone.

whyCorrect: The rival explanation makes the decline depend on workers moving into cities. Districts with almost no such movement are the natural control: if membership falls just as steeply there, urbanisation cannot be doing the work, and the one thing those districts share with the rest is the 1911 scheme. That leaves Kaur's explanation standing.

whyWrong.A: A smaller state benefit would make the state scheme less attractive, weakening rather than supporting the displacement claim.
whyWrong.B: Smaller urban branches fit the rival account about weak city ties.
whyWrong.D: A decline already underway from the 1890s suggests a cause other than the 1911 scheme.

tips: Support for one of two rival causes usually comes from a case where the rival cause is absent but the effect still appears.

whyCorrect: Adeli's claim is that the custom, not the geology, kept the qanats working. Neighbouring valleys with the same geology hold that factor constant, so the only difference left is the absence of the maintenance rule — and their qanats failed within two centuries. That comparison separates the two candidate causes rather than just describing the successful valley.

whyWrong.B: Snowmelt recharge is a geological advantage, which supports the explanation Adeli is arguing against.
whyWrong.C: Clay hoop lining is a construction feature, a third explanation that does nothing for the customary-law claim.
whyWrong.D: When the rule was written down says nothing about whether it kept the tunnels clear during the eight centuries in question.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up two facts: fine sediment settles in annual layers, and each hurricane drops a distinct sand band inside those layers. Together those give a datable sequence in which every storm leaves one countable mark. So a core lets researchers tally storms far back beyond written records.

whyWrong.A: Nothing connects the thickness or presence of a sand band to rainfall; the sand comes off the reef, not out of the sky.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in a sediment core bears on the future path of a storm that has not formed yet.
whyWrong.D: The text says the sand band marks that a hurricane passed, not how hard the wind blew; no wind measurement is described.

whyCorrect: The text supplies one measurable fact about the treeline trees' rings — they can be thinner than a sheet of paper — and then says the lower-slope trees of the same species grow far faster. Faster growth means more wood laid down each year, so wider rings. The completion that follows from what is actually stated is that their rings are easier to distinguish and count.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text concerns how long either group of trees lives; the thousand-year figure describes how long a dead trunk stands, not a lifespan.
whyWrong.B: Decay resistance is credited to dense, resinous wood produced by slow growth, so faster growth points the other way.
whyWrong.C: This directly reverses the passage, which ties density to the treeline trees' very slow growth.

commonMistakes: Filling the blank with something you know about bristlecones from elsewhere instead of what these four sentences establish.

whyCorrect: "The first woman appointed to a full professorship in mathematics in northern Europe" is an appositive renaming Sofia Kovalevskaya, and it is already opened with a comma after her name. A non-essential appositive has to be closed with a matching comma before the sentence continues to its verb. The second comma restores the pair.

whyWrong.A: Leaving the appositive unclosed strands the opening comma and runs the description straight into the verb.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, and "won the Bordin Prize in 1888" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.D: A colon would announce that what follows explains or lists something, and it also cuts the subject off from its verb.

tips: An appositive set off with a comma on one side must be closed with a comma on the other.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence, and everything after it is a list of the goods just referred to: salt, gold and books. A colon is the mark that follows a complete statement to introduce the list that spells it out. That is exactly the relationship here.

whyWrong.A: "But" signals contrast, and the items are not opposed to the wealth — they are what it consisted of.
whyWrong.B: "And" makes the salt read as one more thing alongside the inventory rather than as the content of the list.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and "salt cut from the desert mines, gold ... and books ..." is a list of noun phrases with no verb.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "When," which makes the first half a subordinate clause; the main clause is "they can be seen far to the south." An introductory subordinate clause is joined to the main clause with a comma. Nothing heavier is allowed, because the first half cannot stand alone.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon demands two independent clauses, and the "When" clause is not independent.
whyWrong.C: A colon also requires a complete statement before it, which the "When" clause is not.
whyWrong.D: "And" would try to coordinate a subordinate clause with a main clause, which leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

whyCorrect: "Although the papyrus fragment carries no date of its own" is a concessive subordinate clause, so it cannot stand as a sentence and cannot take a semicolon or colon. Introductory subordinate clauses attach to the main clause with a comma. The comma is the only option that keeps the sentence intact.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and the "Although" clause is dependent.
whyWrong.B: A colon requires a complete statement in front of it and announces an explanation or list, neither of which fits.
whyWrong.C: Adding "and" leaves "Although" governing both halves, so the sentence never reaches a main clause.

whyCorrect: The two faults are joined by "and," and the first is written as "for using undocumented welds." Whatever follows the second "for" has to take the same grammatical form, an -ing verb form serving as the object of the preposition. "Misreporting" makes the pair parallel.

whyWrong.A: "Having misreport" is not a possible verb form in English; "having" would need a past participle after it.
whyWrong.B: An infinitive cannot follow the preposition "for," and it also breaks the parallel with "using."
whyWrong.D: "It misreported" makes a clause, which cannot serve as the object of "for" in this construction.

whyCorrect: The sentence gives two past moments: the flooding in January and the inspectors' arrival in March. The fall in water level happened before the March arrival, and "By the time" marks that ordering explicitly. The earlier of two past events takes the past perfect, "had fallen."

whyWrong.B: The present progressive puts the falling in the present, contradicting the January and March dating.
whyWrong.C: The simple present describes a general or current fact, not an event completed before a past arrival.
whyWrong.D: The future tense points forward from now, which cannot describe what the inspectors found in March.

whyCorrect: The subject is "collection," a singular noun; the phrase "together with its several thousand lichen specimens" is a modifier set off by commas and never changes the number of the subject. The work is finished, having been done over the winter, so the verb must be singular and past. "Was" is the only form that is both.

whyWrong.A: "Have been" is plural and agrees with the lichen specimens inside the modifier rather than with "collection."
whyWrong.B: "Were" is past but plural, so it fails agreement with the singular subject.
whyWrong.C: "Are" is both plural and present, disagreeing in number and in time with a job completed over the winter.

commonMistakes: Treating "together with" like "and"; it adds information without making the subject plural.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives aerogel's advantages: it is the lightest solid ever made and insulates as well as a course of bricks. The second gives the flaw that has kept it out of buildings anyway. The blank has to mark the turn from a strength to the weakness that cancels it.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" would present the crumbling as a result of the insulating performance, which makes no sense.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" adds a similar point, but the second sentence undercuts the first.
whyWrong.C: "For example" would make the fragility an instance of good insulation.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the eruption dimmed sunlight across the northern hemisphere. The second reports frost in every month of the following New England summer, which is what dimmed sunlight would produce. The relationship is cause to effect, so a resultative transition is needed.

whyWrong.B: "By contrast" would set the frost against the dimming, but the frost is what the dimming leads to.
whyWrong.C: "Similarly" pairs two like items, and one sentence here is the cause of the other rather than a parallel case.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" would say the frost happened despite the dimming, reversing the logic.

whyCorrect: Both sentences describe the same survival strategy in different organisms: a plant that dries out and revives with rain, and shrimp eggs that dry out and hatch when a pool refills. Neither causes the other and neither restates the other. The transition has to mark a parallel case.

whyWrong.A: "In other words" introduces a restatement, but brine shrimp are a separate organism with a separate example, not a rephrasing.
whyWrong.C: "Nevertheless" signals contrast, and the two facts agree rather than conflict.
whyWrong.D: "Consequently" would make the shrimp's eggs a result of what resurrection plants do.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why the observers had to be spread so widely, so the answer must supply a reason, not just a fact about the expeditions. The relevant note is that the Sun's distance is worked out by comparing timings taken from widely separated places. The chosen option states that reason and links it to the actual destinations.

whyWrong.B: The rarity of transits explains why 1769 mattered as an opportunity, not why the observers were sent so far apart.
whyWrong.C: What each observer timed describes the task, not the reason for the spread of locations.
whyWrong.D: Listing the destinations restates the fact the question asks you to explain.

whyCorrect: To explain why the replica exists, the sentence has to link the damage from visitors to the closure and then to the replica. Only one option carries that whole chain: breath causing damage, the 1963 closure, and the replica opening nearby in 1983. The rest give isolated notes with no causal link.

whyWrong.A: The span of years the cave was open is a fact about its history and states no reason for building anything.
whyWrong.B: The algae and crystal growth is half the reason, but with no mention of the replica it does not explain why the replica was built.
whyWrong.C: This describes the replica itself and leaves the "why" entirely unanswered.

whyCorrect: "How effective the approach has proved" calls for a measured result, and the only note that gives one is the Wuhan trial districts cutting peak runoff by about half. The chosen option pairs that outcome with the mechanism that produced it. The other options describe the method or the problem without any result.

whyWrong.B: Conventional paving is the baseline problem, not evidence of the new approach working.
whyWrong.C: Listing the design features describes what sponge cities are made of, not what they achieved.
whyWrong.D: The absorb-and-release description explains the mechanism but reports no effect that could be judged effective.

whyCorrect: The point of the channels and cisterns is storage: water caught in wet spells is held so that supply continues "even through years in which no rain fell at all." The blank therefore needs a word about reliability over time, not about quantity. Dependable is what a stored supply that survives rainless years is.

whyWrong.B: Abundant claims a large quantity, which a desert receiving under fifteen centimetres of rain does not support; the achievement is steadiness, not plenty.
whyWrong.C: Seasonal would mean the supply came and went with the year, the opposite of what the cisterns are for.
whyWrong.D: Intermittent means stopping and starting, which contradicts the clause about years with no rain at all.

whyCorrect: The sentence signals a reversal of the Spanish assumption that the cords were merely decorative, and it then describes the quipu holding censuses, tribute rolls and dates precisely. The blank needs a word for a system of recording information in signs. A notational system is one whose knots and positions stand for values, which is exactly how the first sentence describes it.

whyWrong.A: Provisional means temporary or tentative, but the passage stresses precision and durability of record.
whyWrong.B: Rudimentary would make the quipu crude, agreeing with the mistaken Spanish view the sentence is correcting.
whyWrong.D: Ceremonial is close to the ornamental reading the passage explicitly calls the opposite of the truth.

whyCorrect: The measurement described is of distance, and the blank is followed by "from the Earth by about 3.8 centimetres a year." So the word must describe the Moon moving steadily away. Receding means exactly that.

whyWrong.A: Brightening is about light, not distance, and cannot take the phrase "from the Earth by 3.8 centimetres."
whyWrong.B: Contracting would describe the Moon shrinking in size, not changing its distance.
whyWrong.D: Wobbling implies oscillation with no net movement, which cannot accumulate at a fixed rate per year.

whyCorrect: The two facts before the semicolon are that few weavers ever learned the technique and that one family now practises it. "Thus all but" asks you to state the endpoint those facts are approaching. A craft down to a single household is on the verge of dying out, which is what extinct names.

whyWrong.A: Commercial describes trade, and the sentence is about how few people can still do the work.
whyWrong.B: Renowned describes fame, which does not follow from the craft's near-disappearance and does not fit "all but."
whyWrong.C: Mechanised contradicts the description of a hand technique known to almost nobody.

whyCorrect: The blank must be supported by the process just described: repeated simmering, many separate smokings, a deliberate mould inoculation, all over most of a year. Those are demanding, precisely controlled steps. Exacting names a process that requires that kind of care, which is why machinery cannot rush it.

whyWrong.A: Recent contradicts the picture of a long-established traditional method and gives no reason machinery would fail.
whyWrong.C: Lucrative concerns profit, which the passage never raises and which would not prevent mechanisation.
whyWrong.D: Obscure means little known, but being little known is not what stops a process from being hurried.

whyCorrect: The sentence before explains the technique of matching rings to Alpine chronologies, and the sentence after gives a result: violins with eighteenth-century labels containing wood felled a century later. The underlined sentence sits between them and supplies the rule that turns a ring date into a verdict — no instrument can predate its youngest ring. That is the principle that makes the evidence conclusive.

whyWrong.A: The example of mislabelled instruments is the sentence that follows, not the underlined one, which names no instrument.
whyWrong.C: It concedes nothing; it states the strength of the method rather than a limitation.
whyWrong.D: How the chronologies were assembled is covered in the previous sentence, which mentions thousands of Alpine trees.

whyCorrect: The text moves through a clear arc: guano becomes the most valuable fertiliser available, ships queue and two governments fight over it, the deposits are exhausted, substitutes take the market, and the islands are left to ornithologists. That is a rise, a collapse, and an epilogue about the source. No argument or comparison is being advanced along the way.

whyWrong.B: Synthetic ammonia is mentioned only as what replaced guano; no claim about sustainability is made.
whyWrong.C: Labour on the islands is never discussed.
whyWrong.D: The text says guano was the most effective fertiliser but never explains any chemistry behind that.

whyCorrect: The passage builds a chain of dependence: leaves feed the fungus, the fungus feeds the colony, a mould threatens the fungus, and a bacterium the ants carry suppresses the mould. The last clause seals it — remove the bacterium and the garden fails. The main idea has to include both the cultivated fungus as the food source and the bacterium as its protection.

whyWrong.A: The first sentence says outright that the ants do not eat the leaves.
whyWrong.C: The text says the mould would overrun the garden if unchecked, not that it has actually collapsed colonies.
whyWrong.D: The bacterium is protective; the fungus is what the colony eats.

whyCorrect: The second sentence states the function directly and rules out the obvious misreading: the vault does not collect seed in its own right but holds duplicates, so a gene bank destroyed by war, fire or accident can be restocked. The Syrian withdrawal is an instance of exactly that. So its function is backup storage for other collections.

whyWrong.A: Collecting species no one else holds is precisely what the text says the vault is not for.
whyWrong.C: The single withdrawal went to a displaced seed collection, not to farmers, and no distribution role is described.
whyWrong.D: The text says depositors keep ownership of their own boxes.

whyCorrect: Drifting seed capsules could plant a crop, but they could not carry a word. A shared name on both sides of the ocean requires people who had contact with the plant in America to have brought both the plant and its name home. That is evidence only the voyaging explanation can account for, which is what makes it decisive between the two.

whyWrong.A: Growing well in Pacific soils explains why the plant survived once there, under either account of how it arrived.
whyWrong.B: Variety in South America establishes the plant's homeland, which both explanations already accept.
whyWrong.C: Seawater viability of the capsules is what the rival drifting account needs, so it supports the other side.

tips: When two explanations predict the same physical outcome, look for evidence that only one of them could produce — here, a transmitted word.

whyCorrect: Oyelaran claims the crest is for display to other members of the species rather than for steering. A structure that appears only in adults and is far larger in one sex than the other tracks maturity and sex, which is what a signal used in courtship or rivalry does. A steering surface would be needed by every flying individual regardless of age or sex, so this pattern fits display and not aerodynamics.

whyWrong.A: Variation between species is equally consistent with different flight demands, so it does not decide between the two functions.
whyWrong.C: Shared habitats say nothing about what the crest was for in the species that had one.
whyWrong.D: Little added drag removes an objection to the rudder idea and so does nothing for the display claim.

whyCorrect: Ferrer says the compound is an insect deterrent; the colleague says it is a sunscreen. Ultraviolet exposure is unchanged by netting, so if plants shielded from insects make far less of the compound, its production is tracking insect pressure and not sunlight. That result is what the deterrent explanation predicts and the ultraviolet explanation does not.

whyWrong.A: Upper leaves are both the most sun-exposed and the most exposed generally, so this fits the ultraviolet account at least as well.
whyWrong.B: Concentration in the outer cell layers is where a screen against light would sit, favouring the colleague.
whyWrong.C: Strong ultraviolet absorption is the mechanism the rival explanation requires.

whyCorrect: Coppicing gives repeated crops for centuries, while felling gives more wood once and ends the stool. A manager who looks only at the volume taken in a single year sees the larger felling figure and none of the centuries of future crops that felling forfeits. Judged that way, felling looks better than it is over the long run.

whyWrong.A: A single-year measure captures the felled hazel's yield in full; it is the coppice's future yield that goes unmeasured.
whyWrong.C: The text says felling yields considerably more wood at once, so coppicing loses on a single year's volume.
whyWrong.D: The passage states plainly that a coppiced stool throws up fresh poles from the surviving root.

whyCorrect: The worms have no mouth and no gut, so all their food comes from the internal bacteria, and those bacteria build sugars from hydrogen sulphide streaming out of the vent. If the vent stops flowing, the sulphide stops, and with it the only input the bacteria have. The completion has to name that loss of the chemical raw material.

whyWrong.A: An adult worm has neither mouth nor gut, so filter feeding is not available to it.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text suggests adult tubeworms can move; they are described as anchored in crowds around a vent.
whyWrong.D: The colony lives far below any sunlight, which the first sentence states.

whyCorrect: "The pit behind the fort's granary produced three things the archaeologists had not expected" is a complete sentence, and what follows is the list of those three things. A colon is the mark that follows a complete statement and introduces the list it has just promised. The announcement of "three things" is the clearest possible signal for it.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a shoe, a tablet and a barrel of oysters form a list of nouns with no verb.
whyWrong.C: "And" makes the shoe an additional item alongside the three things rather than the first of them.
whyWrong.D: "Which are" with no comma creates a garbled restrictive clause and loses the clean introduction the sentence sets up.

whyCorrect: "He opened the upper paddles a little before dawn" and "the barge was through the lock and moored below the town by noon" are both complete sentences with their own subjects and verbs. Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma or by nothing at all. The semicolon is the only mark offered that can join them.

whyWrong.B: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: A colon signals that what follows explains or itemises what came before; the second clause reports a later event rather than explaining the first.
whyWrong.D: Running the clauses together with no punctuation produces a fused sentence.

whyCorrect: Both halves stand on their own: the balloon rose for forty minutes, and the burner went out and the basket dropped. "Then" is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot rescue a comma between two full clauses. A semicolon is required.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation at all the two clauses are fused.
whyWrong.C: "Then" does not license a comma splice; a comma plus an adverb still leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma.
whyWrong.D: A colon would announce that the second clause explains the first, but it reports what happened next instead.

commonMistakes: Treating adverbs like "then," "however" and "therefore" as if they were conjunctions such as "and" or "but."

whyCorrect: "A moon barely five hundred kilometres across" is an appositive describing Enceladus, and it has already been opened with a comma. The main verb of the sentence, "vents," comes after it, so the appositive must be closed with a second comma before that verb. Only the comma keeps the pair balanced.

whyWrong.A: With no closing mark the appositive runs into the verb and the opening comma is left unmatched.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "vents plumes of water vapour ..." has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.D: A colon also cuts the subject off from its verb and wrongly announces an explanation.

whyCorrect: With a "neither ... nor" subject, the verb agrees with whichever element sits closer to it. The nearer element here is "the firing schedules," which is plural. The sentence also refers to notebooks that survive from a pottery closed in 1924, so the past plural "were" is the form that fits both agreement and time.

whyWrong.A: "Is" is singular and present, agreeing with "recipe" rather than the nearer plural and putting the fact in the wrong time.
whyWrong.B: "Was" is past but singular, so it disagrees with "the firing schedules."
whyWrong.D: "Has been" is singular, and the present perfect also clashes with the fixed, closed-off past the passage describes.

whyCorrect: "All four" tells you the noun is plural, and the air supply belongs to those divers, so the form must be a plural possessive. A plural noun ending in -s takes an apostrophe after the s. That gives "divers'."

whyWrong.A: "Diver's" is singular possessive, which contradicts "all four."
whyWrong.C: "Divers's" doubles the possessive marker; a plural already ending in -s takes only the apostrophe.
whyWrong.D: "Divers" without an apostrophe is a plain plural and leaves "air supply" with nothing to attach it to.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with the participial phrase "Having been rebuilt twice since the earthquake of 1908," which modifies "the campanile" but is not itself a verb. That leaves the sentence needing a finite main verb, and the surrounding sentences are in the present tense. "Retains" supplies the present-tense main verb the sentence lacks.

whyWrong.A: An infinitive is not a finite verb, so the sentence would remain a fragment.
whyWrong.B: "Having retained" is a second participle stacked on the first, leaving no main verb.
whyWrong.C: "Retaining" is also a participle and produces the same fragment.

tips: When a sentence opens with a long participial phrase, check that a real conjugated verb still appears later.

whyCorrect: The first sentence reports a large improvement: potholes down by four fifths. The second reports that complaints about the road went up in the same period, which is the opposite of what the improvement would lead you to expect. The transition must mark that unexpected reversal.

whyWrong.A: "That is" introduces a restatement, but rising complaints are not another way of saying potholes fell.
whyWrong.B: "Accordingly" presents the second fact as the natural result of the first, which is exactly what it is not.
whyWrong.D: "Indeed" strengthens or confirms the preceding claim; here the second sentence pulls against it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a benefit: desalination supplies most of the region's drinking water. The second gives an unwelcome side effect, brine sinking and smothering seabed animals. The transition has to mark the shift from benefit to damaging consequence.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" adds a parallel point, but the second sentence contrasts with the first rather than matching it.
whyWrong.B: "For instance" would make the brine damage an example of supplying drinking water.
whyWrong.C: "In summary" announces a recap, and the brine is new information.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences supply the premises: pollen records what was flowering when the soil was sealed, and this mound's pollen comes from high-summer flowers. The third draws the dating conclusion those premises license. That calls for a transition marking inference.

whyWrong.A: "Admittedly" concedes a point against the argument, but the final sentence is the argument's conclusion.
whyWrong.B: "Conversely" signals an opposite case, and nothing here is reversed.
whyWrong.D: "Meanwhile" marks simultaneous events, not a conclusion drawn from evidence.

whyCorrect: A correction requires naming the mistaken belief and setting the fact against it. The note that supports one is that the object is embroidered in wool on linen rather than woven, which is what a tapestry by definition is. The chosen option states the common assumption and then corrects it; the other options only report facts nobody misunderstands.

whyWrong.A: The comet in the border is a striking detail but corrects nothing.
whyWrong.B: The date of the conquest is uncontroversial background.
whyWrong.C: Length and subject matter are accurate but raise no misunderstanding to correct.

whyCorrect: The goal is mutual support, so the sentence has to show each crop doing something for the others. Only one option gathers all three contributions: the maize stalk as a climbing frame, the beans adding nitrogen, and the squash leaves suppressing weeds. Each of the other options isolates a single plant.

whyWrong.A: Squash shade alone covers one crop and shows no support between them.
whyWrong.B: Planting them in one mound states the arrangement without explaining any benefit.
whyWrong.D: Nitrogen from bean roots is one contribution of the three and leaves the interaction unexplained.

whyCorrect: The question asks how the plots stay productive with no irrigation, so the answer must connect a cause to that outcome. The canals on every side are what keeps the soil wet, and the wet soil is what allows several crops a year. The chosen option states that causal chain; the others give facts with no link to water supply.

whyWrong.B: Willow roots hold the plot together structurally, which is a different problem from keeping the soil moist.
whyWrong.C: Several crops a year is the outcome restated, with no explanation of how it is achieved.
whyWrong.D: How the plots were built up from lake mud describes their construction, not their water supply.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence says the container mattered less as a box than as a standard: cranes, chassis, wagons and hulls were all rebuilt to one set of dimensions. The final sentence contrasts the blank with any property of the steel, so the word must name a relational quality rather than a material one. Interchangeable is what one uniform dimension makes a box, and it is what lets every other piece of equipment be rebuilt around it.

whyWrong.B: Durability is a property of the steel, which the sentence explicitly sets aside.
whyWrong.C: Spaciousness is also a property of the box itself and explains nothing about the rebuilt cranes and wagons.
whyWrong.D: Cost is never mentioned, and cheapness would not require the rest of the system to be redesigned.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence spells out what the harbour gangs do: they decide who may set traps, how many and where, and they enforce those limits. The final sentence places the blank between free access and state control, so it must name limited access allocated by the fishermen themselves. Rationed is the word for access parcelled out under a limit.

whyWrong.A: Abandoned would mean nobody controls the ground, which is the open-access case the passage calls an exception.
whyWrong.B: Advertised concerns publicity and says nothing about who is allowed to fish.
whyWrong.C: Subsidised concerns payment or support and has no bearing on the limits described.

whyCorrect: The argument turns on cycle lengths lining up. A predator peaking every two, three or four years almost never hits the same year as a thirteen- or seventeen-year emergence, because those numbers are prime and share no factor with the shorter cycles. The blank needs a word for two events falling in the same year, which is coincide.

whyWrong.A: Interfere describes disruption between things, not two cycles landing on the same year, and it takes the wrong sense with "peak."
whyWrong.C: Alternate would mean the two take turns, which is a pattern, not the failure to line up that primes produce.
whyWrong.D: Compete describes a contest between the predator and the cicadas, not the timing relationship the sentence is about.

tips: Fill the blank from the mechanism the passage explains, here the arithmetic of matching cycles, not from a word that merely sounds ecological.

whyCorrect: The blank sits inside a "what looks X is in fact Y" frame, so it must name the false impression that the real explanation overturns. The real explanation is deliberate choices made stitch by stitch with the material at hand. The impression it corrects is that the angled strips and abrupt colour changes happened by chance, which is what accidental names.

whyWrong.A: Improvised is close to what the quilts actually are, so it does not stand in opposition to the second half of the sentence.
whyWrong.B: Traditional contradicts the point that the makers rejected the repeating catalogue patterns.
whyWrong.D: Laborious describes effort, and the sentence's correction is about intention rather than how much work was involved.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts flat ground, where one reading covers a wide area, with ground where the instrument must be moved every few hundred metres. What changes between them is how much the land rises and falls. Relief in surveying means precisely that variation in surface height.

whyWrong.A: The easing of pain has no bearing on how often a survey instrument must be repositioned.
whyWrong.B: Aid to people in need is a different sense entirely and cannot be described as "broken" across a plateau.
whyWrong.D: The sculptural sense refers to carving on a flat background, not to terrain.

whyCorrect: The text does two things and only two: it traces the instrument's origin in surplus oil drums and the discovery that a dented head sounds several notes, and it describes the making, sinking the head and hammering a facet for each pitch. The closing line about shaping rather than fitting the note extends the second of these. Origin plus method is the whole of the passage.

whyWrong.A: No claim about orchestral standing is made anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.B: No other Caribbean percussion instrument is mentioned, so nothing is compared.
whyWrong.C: The drums are noted as left on the wharves after the war, but why they were plentiful is never explained.

whyCorrect: The sentence before introduces Iceland spar and its two beams; the sentence after reports a physical find. The underlined sentence bridges them by explaining the actual procedure and why it works: match the beams, read off the plane of polarisation, and that plane points back to the hidden sun. Its job is to show how the sunstone would locate the sun.

whyWrong.A: It raises no doubt about the sagas; it explains how their claim could be true.
whyWrong.B: The wreck recovery is the following sentence, and no circumstances of it appear in the underlined text.
whyWrong.C: No other crystal is mentioned, so no comparison is drawn.

whyCorrect: The last sentence gives the reason in a "because" clause: the terraced ground lower down now held the water that used to run off it. More water retained on the remaining land raised its yield enough to offset the retired slopes. That is the mechanism the question asks for.

whyWrong.A: The text says sediment reaching the river fell; it never says sediment was recovered and spread on fields.
whyWrong.B: Farmers were paid to retire the slopes, but the passage does not say they were paid in grain, and payment would not keep output up.
whyWrong.D: The productivity of the steep slopes is never assessed; the text credits the water held lower down instead.

whyCorrect: The text contrasts two designs by asking whom each suits. Raised letters were shaped so a sighted teacher could read them at a glance; Braille's cell is sized to sit under a fingertip and can be written as well as read by a blind person. The main idea is that Braille designed for the blind user's hand rather than the teacher's eye.

whyWrong.B: The first sentence says embossed alphabets already existed when Braille was a student, so the order is the reverse of this.
whyWrong.C: The existence of earlier embossed alphabets means blind readers did have a means of reading, however awkward.
whyWrong.D: The last sentence says schools resisted the system for decades.

whyCorrect: Hartmann's claim is a negative one: the pull is not merely inattention. Warning people about the effect and paying them for accuracy removes the inattention explanation, because those participants are both alerted and motivated. If they are pulled just as strongly anyway, something other than failing to pay attention is producing the effect.

whyWrong.A: Longer response times to implausible numbers show effort, but they say nothing about whether the pull survives when attention is secured.
whyWrong.B: Experts being less susceptible speaks to who is affected, not to whether the mechanism is inattention.
whyWrong.D: That larger numbers produce larger estimates just restates the effect the first sentence already describes.

commonMistakes: Picking the option that demonstrates the effect exists when the argument is about what causes it.

whyCorrect: Bakker says the breakthrough was organisational, not mechanical. Evidence that the necessary mills existed a century earlier removes machinery as the limiting factor, and evidence that no lake of that size was drained until the companies formed puts the change at the moment the organisation appeared. The two halves together separate the candidate causes in time.

whyWrong.A: Peat cutting explains why the lakes were there, not what made draining them possible.
whyWrong.C: A movable cap is a mechanical refinement, which supports the explanation Bakker rejects.
whyWrong.D: Profitability shows the projects were worth doing but not what made them feasible.

whyCorrect: Two candidate causes changed at the same time, warming and the end of grazing, so support has to come from a case where they are separated. Slopes that kept the same grazing intensity while warming just as much are exactly that case, and the treeline there did not move. That isolates grazing as the factor doing the work.

whyWrong.A: A measured temperature rise documents the rival cause rather than ruling it out.
whyWrong.B: Better seedling survival in warm years supports the warming explanation.
whyWrong.C: That grazers eat seedlings supplies a plausible mechanism for Virtanen but leaves the warming explanation untouched, so it does not decide between them.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up a stalled process: the plant matter never rotted only because freezing stopped the soil organisms, and those organisms are still there and start feeding again once the soil thaws. Thawing therefore restarts the decomposition that was interrupted, and decomposition puts the stored carbon back into circulation. That is the completion the three preceding sentences build toward.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text concerns uptake by living plants; the subject is what the soil organisms do.
whyWrong.B: No mechanism is described that would move the carbon downward, and the material is described as locked in place.
whyWrong.C: This denies the point the passage has just established, that the organisms resume feeding on thawing.

whyCorrect: Every fact given is about work that only people can do: three stigmas per flower, a few days of flowering, picking at dawn, and no machine able to extract the stigmas. "Therefore" asks you to draw the price conclusion from those facts. What they add up to is a very large amount of hand labour behind each gram.

whyWrong.B: Storage is never mentioned; the difficulties described are all in harvesting.
whyWrong.C: Demand could raise a price, but the passage supplies no information about who buys saffron or how much.
whyWrong.D: The area of land the crocus tolerates is never discussed, and the constraint described is labour, not ground.

whyCorrect: The sentence begins with "Because," so everything up to the blank is a subordinate clause and the main clause is the one about herders opposing developments. An introductory subordinate clause is joined to its main clause by a comma. That is the only mark that works here.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon has to join two independent clauses, and a clause opening with "Because" cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.B: A colon needs a complete statement before it, and what follows is not an explanation or list being introduced.
whyWrong.C: Adding "and" leaves "Because" governing both halves, so the sentence never arrives at a main clause.

whyCorrect: What follows the blank, "each of which can be tied to the same reversal," is a relative clause built on "which," so it has no independent standing. A non-essential relative clause is attached with a comma. Nothing heavier is grammatical here.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon requires a full sentence on both sides, and the "each of which" phrase is not one.
whyWrong.B: A colon introduces a list or an explanation after a complete statement, not a relative clause.
whyWrong.C: A period turns the relative clause into a fragment standing on its own.

whyCorrect: "Scholars eventually recognised the marks scratched on them as an early form of Chinese writing" is complete, and so is "the bones turned out to be the divination records of a dynasty." Two independent clauses need a semicolon, a period, or a comma with a coordinating conjunction. The semicolon is the only one of those offered.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two clauses fuse into one run-on.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by "and" is not a legal construction; the colon already performs the join.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences: the material weighs about a fifth of what a concrete slab weighs, and a building framed in it can stand on lighter foundations. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma goes in front of the conjunction. That gives comma plus "and."

whyWrong.A: A colon cannot precede a coordinating conjunction, and nothing is being introduced.
whyWrong.B: Omitting the comma before "and" leaves two full clauses joined as though they were a compound predicate.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon and "and" duplicate the join; use one device or the other.

whyCorrect: The subject is "Each," not "stations" — "of the twelve weather stations" is a prepositional phrase and cannot supply the subject. "Each" is always singular, so the verb must be singular and, given the surrounding present tense, present. "Has" satisfies both.

whyWrong.A: "Have" is plural and agrees with the noun inside the prepositional phrase instead of the real subject.
whyWrong.C: "Having" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.
whyWrong.D: "Were having" is plural and past progressive, clashing with both the subject and the present-tense description of how the network works.

whyCorrect: The comparison is between two measurements of "the iron content," a singular noun, and the blank must stand in for it before the modifier "measured in the sherds from the western one." The pronoun used for that job with a singular noun is "that." The sentence then reads as nearly double the iron content measured in the western sherds.

whyWrong.B: "Those" is plural, but only one quantity, the iron content, is being compared.
whyWrong.C: "Them" is an object pronoun that cannot take a following participial modifier in this construction.
whyWrong.D: "Which" would start a relative clause describing the eastern measurement and would destroy the comparison.

whyCorrect: Ask what "that" refers back to: not the fen, but "the few lowland sites in the county" — the fen is one member of that group, and the group is what has never been drained. The antecedent is plural, so the verb is plural. "Have never been drained" is the correct form.

whyWrong.A: "Is" cannot combine with "never been drained" to make a grammatical verb phrase in this sentence.
whyWrong.B: "Has" agrees with a singular antecedent, but the relative clause describes the sites, not the single fen.
whyWrong.D: "Having" is a participle and leaves the relative clause with no finite verb.

commonMistakes: Reading "one of the few sites that" as singular; the relative clause describes the whole group, not the one.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the observation, that the higher clock runs fast; the second states the same fact as a general rule about distance from the Earth's mass. Nothing new is added and nothing is contrasted — the second sentence rephrases the first at a higher level of generality. That calls for a restating transition.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" signals a contrast, but the two sentences agree.
whyWrong.B: "For instance" would make the general rule an example of the specific observation, which reverses the direction.
whyWrong.C: "Meanwhile" marks something happening at the same time elsewhere, which is not the relationship here.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives every reason to expect simulation to have replaced the wind tunnel: it is far cheaper and has improved for thirty years. The second says physical testing continues anyway, and gives the reason. The transition must mark that the expected consequence does not follow.

whyWrong.B: "Consequently" would make continued physical testing the result of simulation being cheap and good.
whyWrong.C: "Likewise" adds a matching point, but the second sentence pushes against the first.
whyWrong.D: "In short" announces a summary, and the second sentence introduces new information rather than condensing the first.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes that the cloth is assembled from narrow strips whose patterns must line up across the seams. The second states the consequence for the weaver: the whole design must be settled before weaving starts, because a motif crossing a seam cannot be fixed later. The link is cause to consequence.

whyWrong.A: "Similarly" pairs two like facts, but the second follows from the first rather than matching it.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" would set the two in opposition, and they agree.
whyWrong.D: "Even so" concedes that something holds despite the first sentence, when in fact it is caused by it.

whyCorrect: The goal is the condition the effect depends on, which is the final note: the effect holds only when guesses are made independently. A sentence that emphasises a condition has to state the effect and then attach the condition to it. The chosen option does both; the others report the anecdote without any condition.

whyWrong.A: The number of guesses and the setting are background and state no condition.
whyWrong.C: Galton's expectation and the failure of individual guesses describe the surprise, not what the effect requires.
whyWrong.D: Contrasting individual guesses with the middle value describes the result and stops short of any condition on it.

whyCorrect: The goal is how the apparatus made the measurement possible, so the answer has to name the mechanism that turned an unmeasurably small force into something readable. That mechanism is the twist of the suspended wire, whose angle stood in for the attraction between the balls. The chosen option states exactly that conversion.

whyWrong.A: Calculating the Earth's mass is what the result made possible afterwards, not how the apparatus worked.
whyWrong.C: The gap in Newton's law explains why the measurement was wanted, not how it was taken.
whyWrong.D: The date places the experiment in time and says nothing about the apparatus.

whyCorrect: A limitation needs two things: the achievement and the point at which it stopped short. The nests grew to more than 800 by 1993, but the children then moved into primary schools taught in English, so the immersion ended at the school gate. The chosen option sets those two notes against each other, which is what makes it a limitation rather than a fact.

whyWrong.A: The opening of the first nest and its all-day immersion describe the programme working, with no limit named.
whyWrong.B: The 1975 figure is the problem the nests were created to address, not a constraint on them.
whyWrong.D: The count of nests by 1993 is a measure of success on its own.

whyCorrect: The evidence offered for the blank is that the two forms were once taken for separate species, and the change covers colour, appetite and behaviour all at once. A change big enough to fool taxonomists into splitting one animal into two must be complete rather than partial. Thorough is the word for a change that reaches every aspect of the animal.

whyWrong.A: Gradual is contradicted by "within hours," and slowness would not make the two forms look like different species.
whyWrong.B: Reversibility is never discussed, and it would not explain the mistaken classification.
whyWrong.C: Familiar describes how well known the change is, which the mistaken classification argues against rather than for.

whyCorrect: The middle sentences are a list of ordeals zircon survives: mountain-building, erosion, burial in sandstone, and four billion years, with its uranium clock still sealed. The blank must name the property that survival demonstrates. Indestructible is the word for a mineral that comes through all of that unaltered, and it explains why geologists can trust the clock inside it.

whyWrong.B: Abundance is never mentioned, and being common would not preserve a crystal through re-melting.
whyWrong.C: Transparency is an optical property with no bearing on whether the uranium clock is reset.
whyWrong.D: Recent contradicts the four-billion-year age the passage gives.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets the definition up for you: riverbank clay cracks as it dries unless something coarse is worked into it. The next sentence says these potters used crushed shell and that "what was added" varies by workshop. So the word names the coarse material mixed into the clay before firing.

whyWrong.A: A state of mind cannot be identified in a fired sherd or added to clay.
whyWrong.C: The metallurgical sense applies to steel, and no metal is being worked here.
whyWrong.D: A moderating influence on a dispute is the figurative sense and has nothing to do with pottery.

whyCorrect: The blank is measured by what follows it: a blade cannot be pushed between two stones, and the walls have held for six centuries without mortar. Both facts describe how exactly the blocks were cut and fitted. Precise is the word for that quality of workmanship.

whyWrong.B: Decorative concerns appearance, which does not explain why no blade will fit between the blocks.
whyWrong.C: Recent contradicts the six centuries the walls have stood.
whyWrong.D: Irregular is the opposite of what a joint too tight for a blade implies.

whyCorrect: The proteins are described as fastening onto the first crystals to appear and stopping them growing any further, and the last clause insists they do not warm the fish. So crystals do form; they are simply prevented from getting bigger. Minute is the word for crystals held at that first, tiny size.

whyWrong.A: Uniform describes crystals being alike in shape or size, which is not what arrested growth means.
whyWrong.C: Dissolved would mean no crystals exist at all, but the passage says the proteins act on crystals that have already appeared.
whyWrong.D: Mobile describes movement, and nothing in the passage concerns whether the crystals drift.

whyCorrect: The sentence before gives the analysts' proposal, and the two sentences after work out why it was wrong: engine hits were rare in the data because aircraft hit there never came back. The underlined sentence is the hinge, naming the fact about the sample that ruins the inference. Its function is to state the flaw the rest of the text then unpacks.

whyWrong.A: How the holes were mapped is covered in the first sentence, and the underlined sentence adds no method.
whyWrong.B: The last sentence says the armour went on the engines, so Wald's recommendation was adopted.
whyWrong.D: It undermines the original proposal rather than supporting it, and it cites no statistics.

tips: Function questions are answered by what the sentence does for the sentences around it, not by whether it is true.

whyCorrect: The first sentence reports the behaviour: the alloy springs back to shape when warmed. The underlined sentence says why that happens — two crystal structures, with the switch triggered by temperature rather than force. The sentence after applies the behaviour to stents. So the underlined sentence supplies the explanation between the observation and its use.

whyWrong.B: No limitation is raised; the sentence explains a capability.
whyWrong.C: The equal proportions appear in the first sentence and are never accounted for.
whyWrong.D: The surgical use is the following sentence, about stents opening at body heat.

whyCorrect: Each sentence contributes one part of a single claim: the skeleton is spun from silica without heat or pressure, it is diagonally braced with layers that arrest cracks, and modelling finds almost nothing that could be removed without weakening it.
