Put together, that is a description of an efficient, crack-resistant structure built under ordinary deep-sea conditions. Any answer covering only one detail misses the point.

whyWrong.A: The text never compares silica with engineering alloys; the achievement described is the structure, not the raw material.
whyWrong.B: Growth rate is never mentioned.
whyWrong.C: Engineers are said to have modelled the structure, which is not the same as manufacturing copies of it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence answers the question directly: the orchid is pollinated in Mexico by insects that live nowhere else, so plants taken elsewhere flowered and set nothing. Albius's hand method mattered precisely because it replaced those missing insects. The cause of the failure was their absence.

whyWrong.A: Curing happens after pods form; the problem was that no pods formed at all.
whyWrong.B: The text says the plants flowered, so the soil was clearly adequate for growth.
whyWrong.D: The short opening is why hand pollination must be done on one morning, not why the flowers previously set nothing.

whyCorrect: Ferrari claims the lines were made to be walked rather than looked at. A figure drawn as one unbroken line returning to its start is exactly what a procession route needs, and compaction from heavy foot traffic is direct physical evidence that people walked them. The two details together fit walking and are not explained by viewing.

whyWrong.B: Visibility from surrounding hills supports the rival idea that the figures were made to be seen.
whyWrong.C: Dryness explains why the lines survived, not what they were for.
whyWrong.D: Unfamiliar animals bear on what the figures depict, not on how they were used.

whyCorrect: Two candidate causes are on the table, food supply and freedom from predators. Evidence that the amount of dwarfing tracks island area, a proxy for how much food an island can grow, while showing no relation to predator presence, separates them cleanly. It supports Demir's cause and rules the rival out in the same comparison.

whyWrong.A: Earlier maturity is a consequence often seen in dwarfed populations and does not identify which pressure caused the dwarfing.
whyWrong.B: The size of mainland elephants sets the baseline for the comparison but explains nothing about the islands.
whyWrong.D: Absent large carnivores is the condition the rival explanation relies on, so it favours the other side.

whyCorrect: Ferreira's claim links one trait, the sealed cone, to one condition, short intervals between fires. The evidence that tests it has to measure both together, and fire scars record the intervals independently of the trees' cones. Sealed cones being commonest exactly where the recorded intervals are shortest is that correlation.

whyWrong.B: Longer seed viability is a property of sealed cones in general and does not tie it to any fire interval.
whyWrong.C: Faster growth on burned ground explains why fire-adapted seeding pays off but not why short intervals in particular favour it.
whyWrong.D: Equal squirrel harvesting of both types is a difference the finding rules out, leaving the fire claim untested.

whyCorrect: The argument is set up as an elimination: the only forces on the pendulum are gravity and wire tension, and neither can turn its swing plane, yet the plane appears to rotate. If the pendulum is not turning, the apparent rotation must belong to whatever the observation is made against. That is the building and the ground it stands on, carried round by the Earth's own rotation.

whyWrong.A: Air resistance slows a pendulum but supplies no force that could turn its plane of swing.
whyWrong.B: The wire is part of the pendulum, so turning it would be the pendulum turning, which the first sentence excludes.
whyWrong.D: Spin of the bob about its own axis is a separate motion and would not change the plane in which the pendulum swings.

whyCorrect: The detection depends on a faint blue flash reaching a sensor that may be hundreds of metres away, so the ice itself has to act as the light path. Ice that scattered or absorbed the flash over that distance would leave nothing to time, and without the timing the direction cannot be reconstructed. So the array requires ice of exceptional clarity.

whyWrong.B: The temperature of the ice relative to the bedrock has no bearing on whether light crosses it.
whyWrong.C: Age matters for a climate record, not for optical transparency; nothing in the passage links age to the detector's function.
whyWrong.D: This states the requirement backwards — trapped bubbles scatter light, so bubble-free ice is what the array needs, not what would prevent it.

commonMistakes: Choosing a phrase with the right subject matter but the wrong polarity; the blank follows "could not have been built in ice that was."

whyCorrect: "An association of trading towns that at its height stretched from Novgorod to Bruges" is an appositive describing the League, and it has already been opened with a comma after "League." The main verb of the sentence, "maintained," comes next, so the appositive must be closed with a second comma. Only then does the subject connect properly to its verbs.

whyWrong.A: Without the closing comma the appositive runs into the verb and the opening comma is left unpaired.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, but "maintained its own warehouses, negotiated its own treaties" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.D: A colon wrongly announces an explanation and separates the subject from its verb.

whyCorrect: "The trade needed three things in quantity" is a complete sentence that promises a list, and boats, crews and salt are that list. A colon is the mark used after a complete statement to introduce the items it has announced. The word "three" makes the promise explicit.

whyWrong.A: "And" makes boats an addition to the three things rather than the first of them.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation, "quantity boats" runs two nouns together and the list has no introduction.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and this is a list of noun phrases.

whyCorrect: The interruption "a landslide, a cold night, a heavy rain" is opened with a dash, and because the items inside it already contain commas, only a matching dash can close it cleanly. The sentence then resumes with its main clause about the gas coming out of solution. Paired punctuation has to match at both ends.

whyWrong.B: A comma cannot close a dash, and it would also read as one more item in the list rather than the end of the interruption.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon would need an independent clause before it, but the list interrupts a subordinate "If" clause.
whyWrong.D: A colon likewise requires a complete statement in front of it and cannot close a dash.

whyCorrect: "Although the dome of the Selimiye mosque at Edirne is wider than the dome of Hagia Sophia" is a subordinate clause and cannot stand as a sentence. An introductory subordinate clause joins the main clause with a comma. That rules out every heavier mark.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, and the "Although" clause is not one.
whyWrong.B: A colon requires a complete statement before it, and the second half is not an explanation or a list.
whyWrong.C: "And" leaves "Although" governing both halves, so no main clause is ever reached.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists three purposes, and the first two are infinitives: "to stabilise the roof, to rehang the bells." The third has to take the same form for the list to be parallel. "To open" matches.

whyWrong.A: "Having opened" is a perfect participle, which breaks the parallel and puts the action in the wrong time.
whyWrong.B: "Opening" is a gerund and does not match the two infinitives before it.
whyWrong.D: "It opens" is a full clause, which cannot serve as the third item in a list of purposes.

whyCorrect: Two past moments are given: the silting over the winter and the survey boat's return in June. The narrowing was complete before the June visit, and "By the time" marks that sequence. The earlier of two past events takes the past perfect, "had narrowed."

whyWrong.B: The future tense contradicts the winter and June dating, both of which are already past.
whyWrong.C: The present progressive puts the narrowing in progress now rather than finished before June.
whyWrong.D: The simple present states a general fact and cannot express an event completed before a past arrival.

whyCorrect: The subject is "archive," a singular noun; "along with several hundred lantern slides" is a modifier set off by commas and does not make the subject plural. The move happened last spring, so the verb must be singular and past. "Was" is the only form that meets both requirements.

whyWrong.A: "Are" is plural and present, wrong on both counts.
whyWrong.B: "Have been" is plural and agrees with the slides inside the modifier rather than with "archive."
whyWrong.C: "Were" has the right tense but the wrong number.

tips: Phrases like "along with," "as well as" and "together with" add information without changing the number of the subject.

whyCorrect: The first sentence is favourable: a heat pump moves heat, and even at freezing temperatures there is heat outside to move. The second says efficiency drops precisely when demand is highest. That undercuts the expectation the first sentence creates, so the transition must mark a contrast.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" would make falling efficiency a consequence of there being heat available to move.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" adds a matching point, but the second sentence works against the first.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would make the efficiency drop an example of heat being available in the cold.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes a spike in atmospheric radiocarbon and a steady, well-measured decline since. The second states what that curve makes possible: dating tissue by its radiocarbon signature to within about eighteen months. The dating ability follows from the curve, so a resultative transition is needed.

whyWrong.B: "By contrast" would set the two sentences in opposition, but the second depends on the first.
whyWrong.C: "In other words" signals a restatement, and dating tissue is a new consequence, not a rephrasing.
whyWrong.D: "Nevertheless" would say the dating works despite the curve, when the curve is what makes it work.

whyCorrect: Both sentences describe the same idea in different settings: extra information that carries no new message allows a corrupted signal to be recovered, in one case by a receiver using check bits and in the other by a reader passing over a misprint. Neither causes the other. The transition has to mark a parallel case.

whyWrong.A: "Consequently" would make English redundancy a result of adding check bits to transmissions.
whyWrong.C: "Nevertheless" signals contrast, but the two examples agree.
whyWrong.D: "For example" would make English an instance of data transmission with check bits, which it is not; it is a separate analogous case.

whyCorrect: The goal asks what the twelve receptors appear to be for, so the answer must reach the researchers' interpretation. That means holding together the surprising test result, poorer fine discrimination despite far more receptors, with the proposed purpose, immediate recognition instead of comparison. Only one option carries the whole chain.

whyWrong.B: The discrimination result alone is the puzzle, not the explanation of what the receptors do.
whyWrong.C: The receptor counts set the contrast up but propose no function.
whyWrong.D: Independent eye movement and distance judgement concern a different capability altogether.

whyCorrect: What the experiment demonstrated is not just the resemblance but that a brainless organism reached it, and by a describable process of pruning tubes back to the busiest routes. The chosen option carries the process, the result and the significant fact that no nervous system was involved. The others give a single note each.

whyWrong.A: The resemblance alone omits both how the network was arrived at and the point that the organism has no nervous system.
whyWrong.B: A definition of the organism states no result.
whyWrong.C: The oat flakes on the map describe the setup, not what it showed.

whyCorrect: To show a written source is not sufficient on its own, the sentence has to name its weaknesses and show something else filling the gap. The weaknesses are that the book was compiled two centuries late and is silent on woodland clearance; the pollen cores supply exactly what it omits. The chosen option puts both halves together.

whyWrong.B: The pollen evidence on its own says nothing about the written source or its limits.
whyWrong.C: The general statement that archaeologists combine sources reports the practice without giving the reason.
whyWrong.D: The book's list of settlers describes what it does contain, which is its strength rather than its limitation.

whyCorrect: The blank is set against "merely protective," so it must name something the axolotl does that mammalian wound healing does not. What the first sentence describes is a whole limb rebuilt — bone, muscle, nerve and skin, correctly ordered and sized, with no scar. Regenerative is the word for regrowing lost structure rather than just sealing a wound.

whyWrong.B: Cosmetic concerns appearance only, but the axolotl restores working bone, muscle and nerve.
whyWrong.C: Temporary contradicts a limb that is permanently regrown.
whyWrong.D: Defensive is a near-synonym of protective, so it collapses the contrast the sentence is built on.

whyCorrect: Two facts constrain the blank: the navigator studies the chart ashore and then leaves it behind, and the real knowledge is carried in the head. So the object is not consulted during the voyage; it is a device for fixing that knowledge in memory beforehand. A mnemonic is exactly an aid to remembering.

whyWrong.A: A container would hold the knowledge itself, but the passage says the knowledge is carried in the navigator's head.
whyWrong.B: A substitute would stand in for the knowledge at sea, and the chart is deliberately left at home.
whyWrong.D: A receipt records a transaction, which has nothing to do with learning swell patterns.

whyCorrect: The blank contrasts with "documentary," and the sentence before explains why: no lens appears in any inventory, so the case rests entirely on features of the paintings that are consistent with a lens. That is indirect evidence from which a conclusion is inferred rather than direct record. Circumstantial names precisely that kind of evidence, and it explains why the question remains arguable.

whyWrong.A: Anecdotal evidence means second-hand reports and stories, but the evidence here is physical features of the pictures.
whyWrong.B: Fabricated would mean invented, which nobody in the passage alleges.
whyWrong.D: Conclusive contradicts the final clause saying the question is still argued over.

whyCorrect: The working method described is what supports the blank: one colour mixed once and applied to every panel that needed it before the next was mixed. That guarantees the same colour is literally the same across all sixty panels. Consistent names that sameness, and it is what makes the panels read as one work.

whyWrong.A: Vivid describes intensity, which the mixing method does nothing to guarantee and which would not unify the sequence.
whyWrong.B: Restrained describes a limited or quiet range, but the passage says nothing about how bright or muted the colours are.
whyWrong.C: Unpredictable is the opposite of what a single mixing session produces.

whyCorrect: The sentence says standard practice was to throw a cloudy batch away, and Kwolek had it spun anyway. The blank names what she refused to assume the oddity was, so it has to match that discarding instinct. Worthless is the judgement standard practice made and she declined to make.

whyWrong.A: Reproducible describes whether a result can be repeated, which is not the assumption she rejected.
whyWrong.C: Novel is close to how she actually treated the batch, so it reverses the sense the sentence needs.
whyWrong.D: Hazardous would mean dangerous, but nothing suggests the batch was discarded for safety.

whyCorrect: The first sentence rules a method out: the churches were not built up from the ground. The middle sentences describe what the masons actually did, cutting down and inward from the surface of a single rock. The last two draw the consequence, that nothing was assembled, nothing can be added, and the building is finished when the last chip is removed. That is a three-step structure of denial, description and consequence.

whyWrong.A: No individual churches are named and no carving order is given.
whyWrong.C: Only one account of the method is offered, so nothing is weighed against a rival theory.
whyWrong.D: No king and no reign appear in the text.

whyCorrect: The opening lays out the problem: longitude requires comparing local noon with the time at a known meridian, which requires a clock that survives months at sea. The rest reports that the expected astronomical solution was overtaken by a timekeeper made by a joiner, and that the prize came slowly. The text explains the problem and then who unexpectedly solved it.

whyWrong.B: Lunar tables are described as what the Board expected, not argued to be unworkable.
whyWrong.C: No escapement or clock mechanism is described anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.D: The long argument over the prize is reported in one clause, and the text passes no judgement on the Board's treatment of rivals.

whyCorrect: The decisive detail is the experiment: suppress the queen's scent and other females start developing ovaries within days. That shows the non-breeders were never physically incapable, only suppressed. The final sentence states the conclusion directly — what holds the arrangement in place is the queen's continuing presence, not anatomy.

whyWrong.A: No comparison with other mammals is made, and no uniqueness claim appears.
whyWrong.C: The text describes what happens when the queen's scent is suppressed, which is that other females become fertile, not that the colony collapses.
whyWrong.D: Age is never mentioned as the basis for who does which work.

whyCorrect: The stones do one thing, recorded in the last two sentences: they mark how far the water once came, with no dates and no predictions. The second sentence shows that this backward-looking record worked — villages that stayed above the line survived 2011 and several that had spread below it did not. The main idea joins the modest record to its practical reliability.

whyWrong.A: The text says villages above the line came through intact, so the stones were not the only things left standing.
whyWrong.C: The passage says the stones give no dates and predict nothing, which rules out calculated future wave heights.
whyWrong.D: Several villages had spread downhill in the intervening decades, so the warnings were not universally observed.

whyCorrect: Mwangi's claim is specifically that the butterflies use the sun together with an internal clock. Shifting the clock by six hours under artificial light, while leaving the magnetic field untouched, changes only what a sun-compass would use. If the departure bearing then rotates by the predicted amount, the internal clock is demonstrably part of the steering, which the magnetic explanation cannot produce.

whyWrong.A: Separate wintering grounds for eastern and western populations concern where they go, not how they hold a bearing.
whyWrong.B: Continuing to fly south under complete overcast points away from a sun compass and toward the magnetic alternative.
whyWrong.C: Magnetite in other migratory insects supports the rival mechanism.

tips: The strongest evidence in a two-hypothesis question is usually an intervention that alters one mechanism while leaving the other alone.

whyCorrect: Silva claims the effect is about the effort of the form, not about employees reading the default as advice. Telling employees in writing that the default carries no recommendation removes the advice reading while leaving the paperwork barrier exactly where it was. If participation still rises just as much, the effort explanation is what remains standing.

whyWrong.A: Higher matching contributions add a financial incentive, which introduces a third explanation rather than testing Silva's.
whyWrong.C: A pattern by age says who responds most, not whether the mechanism is effort or implied advice.
whyWrong.D: Sticking at the default rate for years shows persistence of the effect but does not distinguish the two causes of it.

whyCorrect: The conservator claims the chromium arrived by contact with lacquer rather than being applied to the blades on purpose. A deliberate treatment would be found across the blades regardless of what lay beside them, whereas contact transfer would leave chromium only where lacquer touched the metal. Finding that exact pattern, present at the contact points and absent from weapons buried away from lacquer, is what distinguishes the two accounts.

whyWrong.A: A corrosion-resistant tin level offers a third explanation for the bright surfaces and says nothing about where the chromium came from.
whyWrong.B: Alkaline soil is likewise an alternative reason for good preservation, not evidence about the chromium's source.
whyWrong.C: Widespread use of lacquer makes the conservator's story possible but does not show it happened on these blades.

whyCorrect: Two facts drive the conclusion: the undercount falls on particular kinds of household, and funding formulas pay per head using the census total. A district where those households are concentrated is therefore recorded as smaller than it is, and money follows the recorded figure. It gets less than its actual population would entitle it to.

whyWrong.A: An undercount lowers the recorded population, so it cannot produce more money than the population warrants.
whyWrong.C: Equal funding would only follow if the count were accurate everywhere, which the first sentence denies.
whyWrong.D: No automatic adjustment is mentioned; the formulas are said to run on the census total as it stands.

whyCorrect: The first sentence rules out scarcity outright: aluminium is the most abundant metal in the crust, but locked in compounds. What changed in 1886 was the process for freeing it, and the price collapsed straight afterwards. A price that falls when the extraction method improves was a price set by the cost of extraction.

whyWrong.A: The passage says the element is the most abundant metal in the crust, so rarity was never the issue.
whyWrong.C: A fashion would not end within a decade of a chemical breakthrough, and no change in taste is mentioned.
whyWrong.D: Deposits are never discussed; the difficulty described is chemical, not geological.

commonMistakes: Assuming an expensive material must have been scarce; here the first sentence is put there precisely to block that inference.

whyCorrect: "The board's inventory of the apparatus that replaced it listed three parts" is a complete sentence, and the drum, the prisms and the clockwork train are those three parts. A colon follows a complete statement to introduce the list it has just announced. The word "three" is the signal that a list is coming.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and this is a series of noun phrases.
whyWrong.C: "And" makes the drum an addition to the three parts rather than the first of them.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation at all, "three parts a drum" simply runs together.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences: the assemblies met to rank their priorities, and the delegates argued those rankings out against other districts' claims. Two independent clauses require a semicolon, a period, or a comma with a coordinating conjunction. The semicolon is the only one offered.

whyWrong.B: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With nothing between them the clauses are fused.
whyWrong.D: A colon followed by "and" is not a usable construction; the colon already joins, so the conjunction is redundant.

whyCorrect: "Each bur was covered in hooks fine enough to catch on any loop of thread or hair" stands alone, and so does "the fastener he patented eight years later reproduces those hooks in nylon." Two independent clauses need a semicolon here, since no coordinating conjunction is offered with the comma. The semicolon joins them correctly.

whyWrong.A: A colon cannot be followed by "and"; the two devices duplicate each other.
whyWrong.C: A comma with no conjunction between two full clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: Running the clauses together with no punctuation produces a fused sentence.

whyCorrect: "A student there who went on to run the workshop" is an appositive describing Anni Albers, opened with a comma after her name. The sentence's main verb, "treated," comes after it, so the appositive must be closed with a matching comma. That restores the pair and connects subject to verb.

whyWrong.A: Without the closing comma the appositive runs straight into the verb and the opening comma is unmatched.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, and "treated the loom as an instrument for research" has no subject.
whyWrong.D: A colon separates the subject from its verb and wrongly signals that an explanation follows.

whyCorrect: With "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with whichever subject is nearer to it, and the nearer one here is "the two volunteers," which is plural. So the verb has to be plural. "Were" is the only plural option offered.

whyWrong.A: "Is" is singular and agrees with "warden" rather than the nearer subject.
whyWrong.B: "Was" is also singular and fails the same agreement test.
whyWrong.D: "Has been" is singular as well, so it cannot agree with "the two volunteers."

whyCorrect: "All three" makes the noun plural, and the notes belong to those supervisors, so a plural possessive is required. A plural already ending in -s takes an apostrophe after the s. That gives "supervisors'."

whyWrong.A: "Supervisor's" is singular possessive, which contradicts "all three."
whyWrong.C: "Supervisors's" adds a second possessive marker that a plural ending in -s does not take.
whyWrong.D: "Supervisors" without an apostrophe is a plain plural and leaves "notes" unattached to an owner.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with the participial phrase "Surveying the ridge in poor light," and whoever or whatever the main clause names as its subject is taken to be doing that surveying. Only people can survey a ridge, so the main clause must begin with the people. "The survey party" is the only subject in the options that can perform the action.

whyWrong.A: This makes "there" the subject and leaves the participle with nobody performing it — a dangling modifier.
whyWrong.B: It says the theodolite was surveying the ridge, which is not what an instrument does on its own.
whyWrong.C: It says the wrong mark was surveying the ridge, which is nonsense.

tips: When a sentence opens with an -ing phrase, check that the noun immediately after the comma is the one actually doing it.

whyCorrect: The sentence before makes a general claim, that departments unrelated to reading have started to use the library's open, no-questions-asked space. The sentence after gives one concrete instance: branches designated as cooling centres on hot afternoons. A single case offered in illustration of a general claim takes an exemplifying transition.

whyWrong.A: "Consequently" would make the cooling centres a result of that trend rather than an instance of it.
whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" signals a contrast, but the example confirms the claim.
whyWrong.D: "In contrast" also demands opposition, and the cooling centres illustrate rather than oppose.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes that the boulder's rock type comes from southern Norway and outcrops nowhere nearby. The second draws the conclusion about the route the ice must have taken to bring it to Norfolk. The reasoning runs from evidence to inference, so a resultative transition is needed.

whyWrong.A: "Nevertheless" marks a concession, but the second sentence follows from the first rather than resisting it.
whyWrong.B: "Similarly" pairs two like facts, and here one is inferred from the other.
whyWrong.C: "In contrast" requires an opposition that the two sentences do not have.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes untreated rubber failing at both temperature extremes; the second describes cured rubber holding its elasticity across the whole range. The two materials behave in opposite ways, and the sentence sets them side by side. That calls for a transition of contrast.

whyWrong.A: "In addition" would add another failing of untreated rubber, but the second sentence describes a success of a different material.
whyWrong.B: "For example" would make cured rubber an instance of untreated rubber's problems.
whyWrong.D: "Consequently" would present sulphur curing as an effect of the earlier failure rather than a contrasting outcome; the sentence reports how the cured material behaves, not why it was developed.

whyCorrect: The goal names two things in tension: the poor reception of the 1848 petition and the movement's eventual success. The answer must hold both, so it needs the committee's finding on the signatures and the fact that all but one demand became law within seventy years. Only one option puts the setback and the outcome in the same sentence.

whyWrong.A: The claimed signature count reports the petition without either the committee's verdict or the later success.
whyWrong.B: The committee's count gives the setback alone and leaves the success unstated.
whyWrong.C: The list of demands is background and mentions neither the reception nor the outcome.

whyCorrect: The goal is the effect on prints that survive today, so the sentence has to reach the present-day evidence and explain it. That means contrasting the fading dayflower blue with the stable Prussian blue and stating the consequence: prints from the 1830s onward keep their blues while earlier ones have lost them. The other options stop before that consequence.

whyWrong.A: The dayflower blue alone gives the problem with no statement about which prints survive with their colour.
whyWrong.B: The arrival date and the graded washes describe the pigment without any effect on surviving prints.
whyWrong.D: Hokusai's use of the pigment is an instance and says nothing about what has survived.

whyCorrect: Dating requires organic material found alongside the object, so what matters is whether the head's context survived. Taruga heads were excavated in place with charcoal in the same layer; heads washed out of gravel have lost the layer they came from and any material that went with it. The answer has to state that contrast, and only one option does.

whyWrong.B: That miners found many heads explains how they were recovered but never says why that prevents dating.
whyWrong.C: The general requirement for organic material is only half the reasoning and leaves the Taruga heads unmentioned.
whyWrong.D: The date range of the culture is background, and it is the very thing being established rather than an explanation.
